title: Chapter 14 — Some Reflections On American Manners
paragraphs: At first glance nothing seems less important than the outward form of human actions, yet there is nothing on which men place more value: they grow used to everything except living in a society whose manners are not their own. The influence of the social and political state of a country on its manners therefore deserves serious examination. Manners are generally the product of the very basis of a people's character, but they are also sometimes the result of an arbitrary convention among certain men. Thus they are at once natural and acquired. When certain men perceive that they are the foremost persons in society without contest and without effort—when they are constantly engaged with large matters, leaving the smaller details to others—and when they live in the enjoyment of wealth they did not amass and do not fear to lose, one can suppose that they feel a kind of haughty disdain for the petty interests and practical cares of life, and that their thoughts take on a natural greatness, which their language and their manners reflect. In democratic countries, manners are generally without dignity, because private life there is extremely petty in character; and they are often low, because the mind has few opportunities to rise above the engrossing cares of domestic interests. True dignity in manners consists in always taking one's proper place, neither too high nor too low; and this is as much within the reach of a peasant as of a prince. In democracies all stations appear doubtful. That is why the manners of democracies, though often full of arrogance, are usually wanting in dignity, and, moreover, they are never either well disciplined or accomplished.

The men who live in democracies are too fluctuating for any one group of them to succeed in laying down a code of good breeding and forcing others to follow it. Every man therefore behaves in his own way, and there is always a certain incoherence in the manners of such times, because they are shaped by the feelings and notions of each individual rather than by an ideal model proposed for general imitation. This, however, is much more noticeable at the time when an aristocracy has just been overthrown than after it has long been destroyed. New political institutions and new social elements then bring together in the same places of resort, and often force to live in common, men whose education and habits are still astonishingly dissimilar, and this makes the motley composition of society peculiarly visible. The existence of a former strict code of good breeding is still remembered, but what it contained or where it is to be found is already forgotten. Men have lost the common law of manners and have not yet made up their minds to do without it, but everyone tries to fashion some sort of arbitrary and variable rule for himself out of the remnants of former usages. So manners have neither the regularity and dignity they often display among aristocratic nations, nor the simplicity and freedom they sometimes take on in democracies: they are at once constrained and without constraint.

This, however, is not the normal state of things. When the equality of conditions is long established and complete, since all men hold nearly the same notions and do nearly the same things, they do not need to agree or copy from one another in order to speak or act in the same way. Their manners are constantly marked by a number of lesser diversities, but not by any great differences. They are never perfectly alike, because they do not copy from the same model; they are never very unlike, because their social condition is the same. At first sight a traveler would say that the manners of all Americans are exactly similar; it is only on closer examination that the peculiarities in which they differ can be detected.

The English make fun of the manners of the Americans; but it is curious that most of the writers who have drawn these ridiculous caricatures themselves belonged to the middle classes in England, to whom the same caricatures are perfectly applicable. So these pitiless critics for the most part furnish an example of the very thing they blame in the United States. They do not see that they are mocking themselves, to the great amusement of the aristocracy of their own country.

Nothing is more damaging to democracy than its outward forms of behavior: many men would willingly put up with its vices who cannot stand its manners. I cannot, however, admit that there is nothing commendable in the manners of a democratic people. Among aristocratic nations, everyone who lives within reach of the first class of society commonly strives to be like it, which gives rise to ridiculous and insipid imitations. Since a democratic people has no models of high breeding, at least it is spared the daily necessity of seeing wretched copies of them. In democracies, manners are never as refined as among aristocratic nations, but on the other hand they are never as coarse. Neither the coarse oaths of the populace nor the elegant and choice expressions of the nobility are to be heard there; the manners of such a people are often vulgar, but they are neither brutal nor mean. I have already noted that in democracies no regular code of good breeding can be laid down; this has some disadvantages and some advantages. In aristocracies the rules of propriety impose the same bearing on everyone; they make all members of the same class appear alike, whatever their private inclinations; they adorn and they conceal the natural man. Among a democratic people manners are neither so tutored nor so uniform, but they are often more sincere. They form, as it were, a light and loosely woven veil through which the real feelings and private opinions of each individual are easily discernible. The form and substance of human actions therefore often stand in closer relation; and if the great picture of human life is less embellished, it is more true. So it may be said, in one sense, that the effect of democracy is not exactly to give men any particular manners, but to prevent them from having manners at all.

The feelings, passions, virtues, and vices of an aristocracy may sometimes reappear in a democracy, but not its manners. Those are lost and vanish forever as soon as the democratic revolution is complete. It would seem that nothing is more lasting than the manners of an aristocratic class, for they are preserved by that class some time after it has lost its wealth and power—and also nothing more fleeting, for the moment they disappear, not a trace of them is to be found, and it is hardly possible to say what they were once they have ceased to be. A change in the state of society works this miracle, and a few generations are enough to complete it. The principal characteristics of aristocracy are passed down by history after an aristocracy is destroyed, but the light and exquisite touches of manners are erased from men's memories almost immediately after its fall. Men can no longer conceive what these manners were once they have ceased to witness them; they are gone, and their departure was unseen, unfelt. For in order to feel that refined enjoyment which comes from choice and distinguished manners, habit and education must have prepared the heart, and the taste for them is lost almost as easily as the practice of them. Thus not only can a democratic people not have aristocratic manners, they neither understand nor desire them. Since they have never thought of them, it is to their minds as if such things had never existed. Too much importance should not be attached to this loss, but it may well be regretted.

I am aware that it has often happened for the same men to have very high-bred manners and very low-born feelings: the interior of courts has shown well enough what imposing exteriors may conceal the meanest hearts. But though the manners of aristocracy did not constitute virtue, they sometimes embellished virtue itself. It was no ordinary sight to see a numerous and powerful class of men whose every outward action seemed constantly dictated by a natural elevation of thought and feeling, by delicacy and regularity of taste, and by urbanity of manners. Those manners threw a pleasing illusory charm over human nature; and though the picture was often a false one, it could not be contemplated without a noble satisfaction.
